reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Ichthyosis describes a group of disorders of cornification characterised by persistent, generalised dry, scaly skin, most of which are inherited, though acquired ichthyosis also occurs
Ichthyosis vulgaris is the commonest form, presenting with fine scaling that spares the flexures, associated hyperlinear palms, and a strong link to atopy and filaggrin mutations
X-linked recessive ichthyosis affects males and produces larger, darker (dirty-brown) scales, and may be associated with corneal opacities and, in some, cryptorchidism
Congenital ichthyoses can present dramatically at birth, including the collodion baby encased in a taut membrane and, at the severe end, the harlequin phenotype

Acquired ichthyosis appearing in an adult without a childhood history should prompt a search for underlying malignancy (notably lymphoma), metabolic, autoimmune, or nutritional disease, or a drug cause

Management is largely supportive, centred on regular emollients, keratolytics or humectants to reduce scale, and gentle skin care, with systemic retinoid therapy reserved for severe congenital forms under specialist care
Neonates with severe congenital ichthyosis are at risk of dehydration, temperature instability, infection, and, with a constricting collodion membrane, feeding and breathing difficulty
Genetic counselling and accurate classification through clinical, and where needed genetic, assessment are valuable for families
reference.pathophysiology: The ichthyoses share a defect in the formation or shedding of the stratum corneum, resulting in accumulation of scale and an impaired epidermal barrier. In ichthyosis vulgaris, loss-of-function mutations in filaggrin reduce production of the protein that aggregates keratin filaments and generates natural moisturising factors, causing retention hyperkeratosis and barrier dysfunction. X-linked ichthyosis stems from steroid sulfatase deficiency, leading to cholesterol sulfate accumulation that impairs corneocyte shedding. The congenital autosomal recessive ichthyoses involve mutations affecting lipid processing and cornified envelope formation. Across subtypes, the disrupted barrier drives increased water loss, compensatory hyperproliferation, and inflammation, with the specific molecular defect determining scale pattern and severity.
additionalDifferentials: Atopic dermatitis and asteatotic eczema (dry, scaly skin overlap)
Acquired ichthyosis secondary to systemic disease or drugs
Netherton syndrome and other syndromic ichthyoses
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history and examination, including family history and age of onset, to separate inherited from acquired disease
Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is unclear
Targeted investigation for underlying malignancy or systemic disease when adult-onset acquired ichthyosis is suspected
Biochemical or genetic testing to define specific subtypes (for example steroid sulfatase assessment in suspected X-linked disease)
Neonatal monitoring of hydration, temperature, and electrolytes in severe congenital forms
redFlags: Severe congenital ichthyosis in a neonate with impaired thermoregulation, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and infection risk
Constricting collodion or harlequin membrane restricting respiration, feeding, or limb perfusion
New adult-onset acquired ichthyosis signalling possible underlying malignancy or systemic disease
Signs of secondary skin infection in a compromised barrier
Ectropion, eclabium, or ocular exposure requiring protective ophthalmic care in severe forms
reference.prognosis: Most common inherited ichthyoses, such as ichthyosis vulgaris and X-linked ichthyosis, are lifelong but manageable with regular skin care and compatible with normal life expectancy; severe congenital forms carry significant neonatal risk and lifelong burden, while acquired ichthyosis often improves when the underlying cause is treated.
pitfalls: Overlooking adult-onset acquired ichthyosis as a marker of underlying malignancy or systemic disease
Attributing chronic scaling simply to dry skin or eczema without considering an ichthyosis
Under-treating with insufficient emollient use, allowing scale and fissuring to persist
Failing to anticipate dehydration and infection risk in affected neonates
Neglecting genetic counselling and accurate subtyping for affected families
management: Restore the epidermal barrier with regular liberal emollients combined with keratolytics or humectants (urea, lactic acid, salicylic acid, propylene glycol) to reduce scale
Practise gentle skin care with regular bathing and mechanical descaling while avoiding irritants
Reserve systemic retinoids (acitretin) for severe congenital forms under specialist supervision
Treat secondary bacterial infection and manage associated features such as the atopic dermatitis of ichthyosis vulgaris
For adult-onset acquired ichthyosis, investigate and treat the underlying cause including lymphoma and other malignancy, metabolic, autoimmune, nutritional or drug causes
Provide intensive neonatal care for severe congenital presentations (collodion baby, harlequin phenotype) with attention to hydration, temperature control, electrolytes and infection
Manage within dermatology and offer genetic counselling for inherited subtypes such as filaggrin-related and X-linked steroid sulfatase deficiency
